results.result: Ciliobrevin D exists as an E-isomer stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding. X-ray crystallography of compound 1 and NMR spectroscopy of ciliobrevin D demonstrate that the benzoylacrylonitrile core adopts an E-olefin configuration with a hydrogen bond between N1 and O11, and the structure is consistent in both crystal and solution phases.
results.evaluation: Claims C53–C64 provide converging structural evidence from X-ray crystallography (C53–C56) and NMR spectroscopy (C59–C62) that consistently support the E-isomer configuration and hydrogen bonding stabilization. The bond length measurements, NOESY coupling data, and chemical shift observations all align to support this structural conclusion.

results.result: The authors synthesized tricyclic pyrazoloquinazolinone derivatives as conformationally constrained analogs of ciliobrevins. The synthetic strategy involved adapting established procedures for compounds 2 and 3, and devising a novel convergent route for compound 4 and related analogs using condensation of 2-fluorobenzoic acid methyl ester with 4-cyano-aminopyrazole.
results.evaluation: Claims C47–C48 and C67–C70 describe the chemical synthesis work with appropriate citations and methodological details. The synthetic routes are clearly documented with reaction schemes (Figure 2A–C) and represent standard organic chemistry approaches that are technically sound.

results.result: Compounds 3 and 4 inhibit dynein 2 with potency comparable to ciliobrevin D at 20 µM, while compound 2 shows no inhibition. GFP-dynein 2 was purified and characterized in microtubule gliding assays, showing velocities of 128 ± 14 nm/s under control conditions and 83 ± 10 nm/s with 20 µM ciliobrevin D.
results.evaluation: Claims C71–C77 present biochemical characterization data with appropriate controls, replication, and statistical reporting (mean ± SD). The microtubule gliding assay results are supported by gel filtration and SDS-PAGE purity data (Figure 2D–I), and the ciliobrevin D inhibition is consistent with prior literature (C75).

results.result: Cyclopropyl-substituted pyrazoloquinazolinones (compounds 5–8) show improved structural alignment with ciliobrevin and enhanced potency. Compounds 6 (dynapyrazole-B) and 8 (dynapyrazole-A) exhibit 6–8 fold improved IC50 values (2.9 ± 0.6 µM and 2.6 ± 1.3 µM respectively) compared to ciliobrevin D (20 ± 1.0 µM) in dynein 2 microtubule gliding assays. Cyclization of the scaffold contributes ~6-fold improvement in potency.
results.evaluation: Claims C80–C93 provide comprehensive structure-activity relationship data supported by crystal structures (C80, Figure 3A,C,D), dose-response curves with IC50 determinations (C85–C88, Figure 3G,H), and direct comparison with uncyclized analogs (C92–C93). The statistical reporting includes error estimates and replication (n ≥ 3), and the 6-position substitution pattern shows clear SAR trends.

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A inhibits Hedgehog signaling with an IC50 of 1.9 ± 0.6 µM, approximately 8-fold more potently than ciliobrevin D (IC50: 15.5 ± 3 µM). The compound acts downstream of Smoothened and shows cytotoxicity at concentrations 10-fold above its IC50 after 28 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C94–C100 present cell-based Gli-luciferase reporter assay data with appropriate statistical analysis (mean ± SD, n = 4–5). The mechanism of action inference (C100) is supported by high SAG concentration experiments and consistent with prior ciliobrevin studies. Cytotoxicity observations (C97–C98) provide important context for the therapeutic window.

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A (5 µM) selectively inhibits retrograde intraflagellar transport in primary cilia, reducing retrograde velocity from 421 ± 156 nm/s to 156 ± 107 nm/s while only modestly affecting anterograde transport (694 ± 117 nm/s to 566 ± 116 nm/s). This pattern is similar to dynein 2 loss-of-function in Chlamydomonas and occurs within 5 minutes of treatment.
results.evaluation: Claims C101–C112 present quantitative live-cell imaging data with robust statistics (hundreds of particles, dozens of cilia analyzed). The automated KymographDirect analysis provides objective velocity measurements, and the selective retrograde inhibition pattern is consistent with dynein 2 function. The comparison to genetic loss-of-function (C112) strengthens the mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A inhibition of intraflagellar transport is reversible. Following washout with serum-containing media (10% FBS), both retrograde and anterograde velocities and transport frequencies recover to control levels within 10 minutes. Recovery is more complete with higher serum concentrations, suggesting serum accelerates compound partitioning out of cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C113–C117 demonstrate reversibility with appropriate washout controls and quantitative recovery measurements (Figure 4F,G and supplement 3). The serum-dependence observation (C115–C116) is supported by comparative data at different serum concentrations, though the mechanism remains inferential (C116). This reversibility is important for establishing dynapyrazole-A as a useful chemical probe.

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A inhibits dynein 1 with an IC50 of 2.3 ± 1.4 µM, approximately 6-fold more potently than ciliobrevin D (15 ± 2.9 µM) in microtubule gliding assays. GFP-dynein 1 was purified to >90% purity and moves microtubules at 508 ± 60 nm/s. The inhibition is reversible upon washout.
results.evaluation: Claims C119–C128 provide comprehensive biochemical characterization of dynein 1 inhibition with appropriate protein purity controls (C119–C120, Figure 5A,B), velocity measurements consistent with literature (C121–C122), and dose-response analysis (C125–C127, Figure 5D). The reversibility data (C128) further validates the compound as a chemical probe. Statistical reporting is appropriate (n = 3–5, mean ± SD).

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A suppresses bidirectional lysosome transport in CAD cell neurites at concentrations near its in vitro IC50 (3.5–5 µM). Treatment reduces both velocity and track length of lysosomes in a dose-dependent manner without depleting cellular ATP levels at 5 µM over 3 hours, suggesting specific dynein 1 inhibition rather than general metabolic toxicity.
results.evaluation: Claims C135–C144 present live-cell imaging data of lysosome motility with quantitative velocity and displacement measurements (Figure 5H–O). The ATP stability control (C142–C143, Figure 5 supplement 5) is critical for ruling out non-specific metabolic effects. The bidirectional inhibition is consistent with known dynein-kinesin coupling (C134), though this mechanistic interpretation is inferential (C144).

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A (40 µM) does not inhibit basal ATPase activity of GFP-dynein 1 and only partially inhibits His-dynein 1 (~30%), while ciliobrevin D (40 µM) inhibits both constructs by ~70%. This modest basal inhibition is unexpected given dynapyrazole-A's potent inhibition of microtubule gliding at 20-fold lower concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C145–C153 present a key mechanistic finding with appropriate controls comparing two protein constructs and two inhibitors (Figure 6A,C). The basal ATPase rates are within literature ranges (C149), and the differential inhibition pattern between dynapyrazole-A and ciliobrevin D is clearly demonstrated. The observation is indeed unexpected (C153) and motivates further mechanistic investigation.

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A potently inhibits microtubule-stimulated ATPase activity of dynein 1, with activity saturating at a residual rate of ~0.5 s⁻¹ and an IC50 of 6.2 ± 1.6 µM. This contrasts with ciliobrevin D, which does not show a plateau in dose-response curves up to solubility limits.
results.evaluation: Claims C154–C158 demonstrate selective inhibition of microtubule-stimulated activity with dose-response data across multiple microtubule concentrations (Figure 6D,E). The non-zero plateau (C156–C157) is a distinctive feature suggesting incomplete inhibition or a distinct mechanism. The comparison with ciliobrevin D (C158) highlights mechanistic differences between the two scaffolds.

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A (4 µM) reduces ADP-vanadate-dependent photocleavage of dynein at AAA1 by ~2.5-fold (from 42 ± 3% to 17 ± 2%), consistent with binding at the AAA1 site. Photocleavage fragments are consistent with cleavage at AAA1.
results.evaluation: Claims C159–C162 use an established biochemical assay for AAA1 site occupancy with appropriate controls and quantification (Figure 6F,G). The reduction in photocleavage at a concentration near the IC50 supports AAA1 site binding, though the inference (C162) requires the assumption that photocleavage reduction indicates competitive binding. The n = 3 replication provides adequate statistical support.

results.result: An AAA3 Walker A mutant (K2601A) shows elevated basal activity (1.1 ± 0.2 s⁻¹) and reduced microtubule stimulation compared to wild-type. Dynapyrazole-A (30 µM) strongly inhibits both basal (~70%) and microtubule-stimulated (70–80%) activity of this mutant with an IC50 of 5.5 ± 1.6 µM for basal activity, similar to its IC50 for wild-type microtubule-stimulated activity, suggesting AAA1 is the primary target site.
results.evaluation: Claims C163–C175 present a sophisticated genetic approach to dissect site-specific inhibition. The mutant protein is properly characterized (C163–C169, Figure 6H–J) with gel filtration and activity measurements consistent with literature (C167, C169). The similar IC50 values for mutant basal and wild-type microtubule-stimulated inhibition (C172, C175) provide strong evidence for AAA1 targeting, though this remains an inference (C175). The residual activity at high inhibitor concentrations (C174) suggests incomplete inhibition or additional complexity.

results.result: The pyrazoloquinazolinone scaffold addresses key limitations of ciliobrevins including potential nucleophile reactivity, storage instability, and discrepancies between in vitro and cellular potencies. The dynapyrazole structure has not been previously reported in bioactive compounds, though hydrophobicity remains a limitation requiring further optimization.
results.evaluation: Claims C176–C183 provide a critical assessment of scaffold improvements with appropriate citations for ciliobrevin limitations (C177–C178). The novelty claim (C182) is stated cautiously ('to our knowledge') and the acknowledgment of remaining limitations (C183) demonstrates balanced evaluation. The similar in vitro and cellular potencies (C179) support improved target engagement.

results.result: The differential inhibition pattern suggests that AAA1 contributes minimally to dynein's basal activity, with AAA3 likely accounting for the majority of basal ATPase activity. The AAA3 mutant's elevated basal activity is consistent with a state mimicking activated AAA1 hydrolysis, and AAA3 nucleotide state regulates AAA1 activity in the presence of microtubules.
results.evaluation: Claims C214–C221 present mechanistic interpretations that are largely speculative (C215–C217 explicitly marked as speculation). While the differential inhibition data support some role differentiation between AAA1 and AAA3, the specific contributions to basal activity remain inferential. The regulatory model (C218–C220) is supported by citations but the connection to the current data is indirect. Additional experiments would be needed to definitively establish site-specific contributions to basal activity.

results.result: Conformational restriction of the ciliobrevin scaffold through cyclization afforded ~6–8 fold improvement in potency, but required incorporation of a cyclopropyl spacer rather than direct tricyclization. This unexpected finding that conformational restriction changed both potency and mechanism of inhibition suggests alternative scaffolds might reveal additional modes of dynein inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C225–C228 synthesize the structure-activity relationship findings into a coherent medicinal chemistry narrative. The ~6–8 fold improvement (C225) is supported by IC50 comparisons (C88, C93), and the requirement for cyclopropyl incorporation (C227) is demonstrated by comparing compounds 4 vs 5–8. The speculation about alternative scaffolds (C228) is appropriately framed as a question for future work.

results.result: Bidirectional inhibition of lysosome motility by dynapyrazole-A can be explained by micromechanical coupling between dynein and kinesins, where opposing force is needed to activate directional motion. Dynein depletion reduces bidirectional organelle motion, and this can be restored by adding a minus-end directed kinesin.
results.evaluation: Claims C187–C190 provide mechanistic context for the lysosome motility results through appropriate citations (C187–C189). The explanation for bidirectional inhibition (C190) is inferential but well-supported by prior literature on motor coupling (C188–C189). This represents a reasonable interpretation of the observed phenotype rather than a novel finding.

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A potency is sensitive to protein concentration in solution, likely due to compound hydrophobicity (ClogP: 4.2 for dynapyrazole-A, 4.5 for ciliobrevin D). This sensitivity has been previously noted for ciliobrevin D.
results.evaluation: Claims C129–C132 document an important technical consideration for assay interpretation with supporting data (Figure 5 supplement 4) and appropriate citation (C129). The ClogP values (C131–C132) provide quantitative support for the hydrophobicity explanation (C130), though this remains inferential. This is a methodological observation rather than a primary finding.

results.result: The AAA+ superfamily comprises ~100 proteins in humans that are essential for cellular processes including DNA replication, proteostasis, membrane remodeling, and cytoskeletal organization. Small molecule inhibitors are valuable tools for studying these enzymes, but only valosin-containing protein and dynein have well-characterized antagonists.
results.evaluation: Claims C1–C5 provide appropriate background context with citations and methodology for the protein count (C1). These are established facts from the literature that set up the rationale for the study. The claims are well-supported but represent prior knowledge rather than new findings.

results.result: Dyneins are microtubule-based AAA+ motor proteins divided into axonemal and cytoplasmic classes. Cytoplasmic dyneins 1 and 2 transport diverse cargos at rates >1 µm/s, making fast-acting reversible inhibitors valuable tools for studying dynein-dependent processes including intraflagellar transport and Hedgehog signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C6–C15 provide essential background on dynein biology with appropriate citations. These are well-established facts that motivate the need for improved chemical probes. The inference about inhibitor utility (C15) is reasonable given the timescales involved. This represents literature context rather than new findings.

results.result: Ciliobrevins are the first selective, cell-permeable dynein inhibitors but have limitations including low potency (requiring 50–100 µM for complete inhibition), suboptimal chemical properties, and potential selectivity issues at high concentrations. Prior dynein antagonists like vanadate and EHNA have limited cell permeability or selectivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C16–C24 provide critical assessment of existing tools with appropriate citations. The limitations are well-documented in the literature (C22, C23) and provide clear motivation for developing improved inhibitors. These represent prior knowledge and problem definition rather than new findings.

results.result: Ciliobrevins are based on a benzoylacrylonitrile-substituted quinazolinone scaffold that can isomerize and has potential chemical instability. The preferred isomer has not been determined, and modifications can affect core geometry, making activity-guided optimization challenging. Up to 100-fold potency differences between biochemical and cell-based assays raise target specificity concerns.
results.evaluation: Claims C25–C36 identify specific chemical and pharmacological problems with ciliobrevins through literature citations (C26–C28) and direct observations (C34). These claims establish the rationale for scaffold redesign. The 100-fold potency difference (C34) is a significant concern, though no new data is presented. This represents problem definition rather than new findings.

results.result: Dynein contains six unique AAA domains on a single polypeptide, each with specialized roles. In dynein 1, AAA1 and AAA3 substantially contribute to ATP hydrolysis and are required for motility. Microtubule-stimulated ATPase activity occurs mainly at AAA1, while AAA3 plays a regulatory role. The specific AAA sites modulated by ciliobrevins remain unclear.
results.evaluation: Claims C37–C46 provide essential mechanistic background on dynein's multi-site architecture with appropriate citations to structural and biochemical literature. The uncertainty about ciliobrevin's site of action (C46) motivates the mechanistic studies in this work. This represents prior knowledge that contextualizes the findings.

results.result: A related acylacrylonitrile-substituted quinazolinone favors a Z-olefin conformation at C2-C9, also stabilized by intramolecular hydrogen bonding. This suggests the isomeric preference of the ciliobrevin pharmacophore is sensitive to distal substitutions.
results.evaluation: Claims C57–C58 provide comparative structural context from literature (C57, citation to Milokhov et al., 2013) that supports the inference about substitution sensitivity (C58). This contextualizes the structural findings but represents a minor supporting observation rather than a primary result.

results.result: The authors hypothesized that replacing the benzoylacrylonitrile core with a heterocyclic scaffold maintaining ciliobrevin geometry could improve inhibitors. A tricyclic scaffold could replace the N1-H-O11 interaction, and adding a cyclopropyl spacer would restrict rotation while improving alignment with ciliobrevin.
results.evaluation: Claims C65–C66 and C78–C79 describe the design rationale for the new scaffolds. These are clearly stated as hypotheses and reasoning (C65–C66, C78–C79) that guided the synthetic work. The subsequent experimental results validate these design principles, but these claims represent the design logic rather than experimental findings.

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A is predicted to inhibit dynein 1 like ciliobrevin D, and may be useful for acute inhibition studies and chemical 'separation of function' to distinguish microtubule-stimulated and basal activities. It will be a useful tool for studying ciliary transport and Hedgehog signaling.
results.evaluation: Claims C118, C191, C195, and C222 represent predictions and proposed applications based on the experimental findings. The prediction about dynein 1 inhibition (C118) is validated by subsequent experiments. The utility statements (C191, C195, C222) are reasonable extrapolations from the data but represent prospective applications rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: Dynapyrazole-A blocks both dynein 1 and 2. Dynein 1 plays critical roles in numerous cellular processes, and its persistent inhibition is expected to be toxic to cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C192–C194 summarize key findings (C192) and provide biological context (C193–C194). The toxicity expectation (C194) is supported by ATP depletion data (Figure 5 supplement 5) and is consistent with dynein 1's essential functions. These represent summary statements and biological context rather than primary findings.

results.result: Previous ciliobrevin analogs with tolyl ethers showed modest dynein 2 selectivity at low ATP concentrations, but this selectivity is suppressed at physiological ATP concentrations, possibly by targeting the high-affinity ATPase site. Dynapyrazoles inhibit at high ATP concentrations with a different mechanism, and the tolyl ether selectivity strategy is unlikely to apply to dynapyrazoles. Developing isoform-selective dynapyrazoles will require extensive SAR studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C196–C203 discuss prior selectivity work (C196, citation to See et al., 2016) and its limitations (C197–C199), contrast with dynapyrazole properties (C200–C201), and outline future directions (C202–C203). The mechanistic speculation (C199) is appropriately framed as possibility. This represents discussion of prior work and future directions rather than new findings.

results.result: Three lines of evidence indicate dynapyrazole-A targets AAA1: it blocks ADP-vanadate photocleavage at site 1, inhibits an AAA3 mutant construct where activity is mainly from AAA1, and the AAA1 nucleotide-binding residues are identical between dynein 1 and 2. However, further biophysical and structural studies are needed to confirm binding at or near AAA1.
results.evaluation: Claims C204–C213 synthesize multiple lines of evidence (C207–C211) into a coherent mechanistic model (C212) while acknowledging the need for additional validation (C213). The sequence conservation data (C211) and functional data (C208–C210) provide converging support, though the conclusion remains inferential. This represents mechanistic interpretation of the primary findings.

results.result: Conformational restriction is a well-established strategy for improving ligand potency that typically requires structural data. This approach may be effective for improving AAA+ inhibitors, and compounds with distinct mechanisms of action will be especially valuable for multi-site enzymes with allosteric regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C223–C224 and C229–C230 provide medicinal chemistry context (C223–C224, citation to Babine and Bender, 1997) and propose broader applications (C229–C230). These represent discussion of general principles and future directions rather than findings from this study. The proposals are reasonable but speculative.
